group.title: Common idioms
sources: Words and CEFR levels chosen by the authors from general knowledge of English; meanings, examples and sentences are original

Word-list licences checked 2026-10-25: CEFR-J Wordlist 1.5 (Tono Laboratory, TUFS; free with citation, A1-B2) and NGSL/NAWL (CC BY-SA 4.0) were not copied; Oxford 3000 and English Vocabulary Profile terms were not confirmed, so they were not used

words.meaning: To watch someone or something carefully so nothing goes wrong.
examples: Could you {keep an eye on} my bag while I buy a coffee?
wrong: I kept an eye on the soup, so I had no idea it was boiling over.

words.meaning: To tell someone something untrue as a friendly joke.
examples: Relax, I’m only {pulling your leg} about the extra homework.
wrong: He was pulling my leg, so every word he said was a serious fact.

words.meaning: Suddenly and without any warning.
examples: My old school friend called me {out of the blue} last night.
wrong: The visit came out of the blue because we had planned it for months.

words.meaning: To decide what to do as things happen, without a fixed plan.
examples: We don’t know the weather yet, so let’s {play it by ear}.
wrong: We played it by ear and followed a detailed plan written weeks before.

words.meaning: To get the most attention and praise at an event.
examples: The youngest dancer {stole the show} with her solo.
wrong: She stole the show, so nobody in the audience noticed her at all.

words.meaning: To stay brave and hopeful when things are hard.
examples: {Keep your chin up}; the next exam will go better.
wrong: Keep your chin up and give up hope completely.

words.meaning: Very common and so not special or valuable.
examples: Cheap sunglasses are {a dime a dozen} at the beach.
wrong: This stamp is a dime a dozen; there are only two in the world.

words.meaning: Quick to understand and react; alert and well organized.
examples: Our new assistant is really {on the ball}.
wrong: He’s so on the ball that he forgets every meeting.

words.meaning: News passed from one person to another by talking, not by ads.
examples: The little cafe became popular by {word of mouth}.
wrong: We spread it by word of mouth, using only TV commercials.

words.meaning: To learn how to do something after some practice.
examples: Skiing is hard at first, but you’ll {get the hang of} it.
wrong: I got the hang of driving, so I still can’t start the car.

words.meaning: To leave a place and start a journey.
examples: It’s getting late; we should {hit the road}.
wrong: We hit the road and stayed at home all weekend.

words.meaning: In the same difficult situation as someone else.
examples: Don’t worry about the late train; we’re all {in the same boat}.
wrong: We were in the same boat: I had problems and she had none.

words.meaning: In good times and bad times, always loyally.
examples: My sister has supported me {through thick and thin}.
wrong: He stayed with me through thick and thin, but left at the first problem.

words.lemma: let the cat out of the bag
words.meaning: To tell a secret by mistake.
examples: Tom {let the cat out of the bag} about the surprise party.
wrong: She let the cat out of the bag, so the secret stayed safe.
words.ipa: /lɛt ðə kæt aʊt əv ðə bæɡ/

words.meaning: To accept what happens and not fight against it.
examples: On holiday I just {go with the flow} and see what happens.
wrong: He goes with the flow and argues about every small change.

words.meaning: To wait patiently and not take any action yet.
examples: {Sit tight}; the doctor will see you in a few minutes.
wrong: Sit tight and run outside right now.

words.meaning: Extremely happy and pleased.
examples: She was {over the moon} when she got the job.
wrong: I was over the moon about failing my test.

words.meaning: Practical, sensible and friendly, not proud.
examples: Despite being famous, the actor is very {down to earth}.
wrong: She’s so down to earth that she won’t talk to ordinary people.

words.meaning: Something that has only a small chance of success.
examples: Winning the prize is {a long shot}, but I’ll try.
wrong: It’s a long shot, so it’s sure to happen.

words.meaning: Said in a very short and simple way.
examples: {In a nutshell}, we need more money and more time.
wrong: In a nutshell, let me explain it all in a two-hour speech.

words.meaning: A change in what you think or feel about something.
examples: He had {a change of heart} and decided to stay.
wrong: She had a change of heart and kept exactly the same opinion.

words.meaning: Whatever happens, in any weather or situation.
examples: He walks his dog every morning, {come rain or shine}.
wrong: We’ll play the match come rain or shine, but not if it rains.

words.lemma: have a lot on your plate
words.meaning: To have many jobs or problems to deal with.
examples: I can’t help this week; I {have a lot on my plate}.
wrong: She has a lot on her plate, so she’s bored with nothing to do.

words.meaning: To annoy someone, often by doing something again and again.
examples: That loud ringtone really {gets on my nerves}.
wrong: His calm voice gets on my nerves, so I love listening to him.

words.lemma: on the tip of your tongue
words.meaning: Almost remembered, but you can’t quite say it.
examples: Her name is {on the tip of my tongue}.
wrong: The word was on the tip of my tongue, so I said it at once.

words.meaning: To tell someone about a worry you have kept secret, so you feel better.
examples: I need to {get this off my chest}: I broke your mug.
wrong: He got it off his chest by never telling anyone.

words.meaning: To keep trying and not give up in a hard situation.
examples: {Hang in there}; the training gets easier.
wrong: Hang in there and quit at the first problem.

words.meaning: To be less strict with someone because of their situation.
examples: {Cut him some slack}; it’s his first week.
wrong: The teacher cut us some slack and gave us extra punishment.

words.lemma: give someone the benefit of the doubt
words.meaning: To believe someone even though you are not sure they are honest.
examples: I’ll {give her the benefit of the doubt} and accept her excuse.
wrong: I gave him the benefit of the doubt and called him a liar.
words.ipa: /ɡɪv ˈsʌmˌwʌn ðə ˈbɛnəfɪt əv ðə daʊt/

words.meaning: Unable to decide between two choices.
examples: I’m {in two minds} about taking the job abroad.
wrong: I’m in two minds, so I know exactly what to do.

words.meaning: To not laugh or smile when something is funny.
examples: It was hard to {keep a straight face} when his hat fell off.
wrong: She kept a straight face and burst out laughing.

words.meaning: To not tell someone about something important.
examples: They {kept us in the dark} about the changes.
wrong: They kept me in the dark by telling me every detail.

words.lemma: off the top of your head
words.meaning: Said quickly, without checking or thinking much.
examples: {Off the top of my head}, I’d say about fifty people came.
wrong: Off the top of my head, after a week of research, the answer is ten.

words.meaning: Agreeing about what to do and why.
examples: Let’s meet first so we’re all {on the same page}.
wrong: We’re on the same page, so we disagree about everything.

words.meaning: Someone who feels uncomfortable in a new or strange place.
examples: At the fancy dinner, I felt like {a fish out of water}.
wrong: He felt like a fish out of water in his own comfortable home.

words.meaning: To know every detail of something very well.
examples: She {knows the city inside out}.
wrong: He knows the rules inside out, but he’s never read them.

words.meaning: Something good that makes a good situation even better.
examples: We won the match, and the sunny weather was {the icing on the cake}.
wrong: The rain was the icing on the cake that ruined our picnic.

words.meaning: Said when someone you were just talking about appears.
examples: {Speak of the devil}, here’s Maria now!
wrong: Speak of the devil, here’s someone we’ve never mentioned.

words.meaning: To seem familiar, as if you have heard it before.
examples: His name {rings a bell}, but I can’t remember his face.
wrong: That name rings a bell, so I’m sure I’ve never heard it.

words.meaning: A lot of anger or worry about something unimportant.
examples: The argument over the parking space was {a storm in a teacup}.
wrong: The war was just a storm in a teacup.
